items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch2)** The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture separates the user view from the physical storage. The level describing 'what data is stored and the relationships among it' is the:
items.explain: TB1 Ch2: the conceptual level describes the structure of the whole database (entities, relationships, constraints) hiding physical storage; internal = storage; external = user views.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch2)** 'Program-data independence' — the ability to change a file's storage structure without changing the application programs — is a key characteristic enabled by:
options: Storing the structure description (metadata) in the DBMS catalog, separate from programs
Hard-coding the structure in each program
items.explain: TB1 Ch2: because the DBMS stores the data definition (metadata) in its catalog separately from access programs, the structure can change without recompiling programs — program-data independence.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch3)** In the EER/ER model, an attribute such as `Name` made up of `Fname, Minit, Lname` is called a:
items.explain: TB1 Ch3: a composite attribute can be divided into smaller subparts (Name → Fname/Minit/Lname; Address → Street/City/State/Zip). Multivalued = double oval; derived = dashed oval.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch3)** A weak entity type (e.g. DEPENDENT in the COMPANY database) is identified by:
options: A combination of its partial key and the owner entity's primary key
items.explain: TB1 Ch3: a weak entity has no key of its own; it is identified by its partial key (discriminator) + the identifying owner's primary key. It has total participation in the identifying relationship.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch3)** In the COMPANY database, an EMPLOYEE works for exactly one DEPARTMENT but a DEPARTMENT has many employees. The WORKS_FOR relationship has cardinality ratio:
items.explain: TB1 Ch3: DEPARTMENT:EMPLOYEE in WORKS_FOR is 1:N — one department relates to many employees, each employee to at most one department. (WORKS_ON, employee↔project, is M:N.)

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch9 — ER-to-relational mapping)** When mapping a binary M:N relationship to relations, you:
options: Add a foreign key to one side
Create a new relation (relationship relation) whose key is the combination of both participating entities' primary keys
items.explain: TB1 Ch9 mapping step: an M:N relationship becomes a new relation S whose primary key is the combination of the foreign keys referencing the two entities, plus any relationship attributes.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch9)** A multivalued attribute (e.g. an employee's `Locations`) is mapped to:
options: A new relation containing the attribute plus a foreign key to the entity, with both forming the key
items.explain: TB1 Ch9: for each multivalued attribute, create a new relation R with the attribute + the owner's PK (as FK); the PK of R is the combination — keeping the schema in 1NF.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch6 / Ramakrishnan, Ch4)** The relational-algebra PROJECT operation (∏) eliminates duplicate tuples because:
options: A relation is a set, and sets have no duplicate elements
items.explain: TB2 Ch6: the result of relational algebra is a relation (a set), so ∏ removes duplicates. (SQL, in contrast, uses multisets and keeps duplicates unless DISTINCT is specified.)

items.q: **(Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, Ch4)** Over the Sailors(sid,sname,rating,age), Boats(bid,bname,color), Reserves(sid,bid,day) schema, 'find sailors who have reserved EVERY boat' is naturally expressed using:
items.explain: Ramakrishnan Ch4: 'every/all' queries use division — (∏sid,bid Reserves) ÷ (∏bid Boats) returns sids that appear with every bid in Boats.

items.q: **(Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, Ch4)** To find the **names** of sailors who have reserved a red boat, the correct relational-algebra strategy is:
items.explain: Select red boats, join to Reserves (on bid) and Sailors (on sid), then project sname: ∏sname(σcolor='red'(Boats) ⋈ Reserves ⋈ Sailors). Select rows → join → project columns.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch8)** The aggregate-function operation ℱ in relational algebra, written `R ℱ COUNT(sid), AVG(age) (Sailors)` with R as a grouping attribute, computes:
options: A single count and average for the whole relation
The count and average age computed per group of R
items.explain: TB1 Ch8: the grouping attribute(s) on the left of ℱ partition the tuples; the aggregates on the right are computed per group — equivalent to SQL GROUP BY.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch6)** For r ∪ s, r ∩ s and r − s to be valid, r and s must be:
options: Compatible: same arity (number of attributes) with matching attribute domains
items.explain: TB2 Ch6: union, intersection and set-difference require the relations to have the same number of attributes, with the domains of the i-th attributes matching (union-compatibility).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch3)** In SQL, `numeric(p, d)` specifies a fixed-point number where:
options: p decimals and d total digits
p total digits with d digits after the decimal point
items.explain: TB2 Ch3: numeric(p,d) has p total digits (plus sign) with d to the right of the decimal point. numeric(3,1) stores 44.5 exactly, but not 444.5 or 0.32.

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch6 / Silberschatz Ch3)** The SQL `UNIQUE` clause specifies a(n):
items.explain: TB1 Ch6: UNIQUE specifies alternate (secondary) keys — what the relational model calls candidate keys. PRIMARY KEY specifies the primary key (and implies NOT NULL).

items.q: **(Elmasri & Navathe, Ch6)** A foreign key declared `ON DELETE SET NULL` requires that:
options: The foreign-key columns are part of the primary key
items.explain: TB1 Ch6: ON DELETE SET NULL sets the child FK to NULL when the referenced parent row is deleted — so the FK columns must be allowed to be NULL (cannot also be part of the PK, which is NOT NULL).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch3)** The basic SQL query `SELECT A1, A2 FROM r WHERE P` is equivalent to which relational-algebra expression?
items.explain: TB2 Ch3: SELECT-FROM-WHERE = ∏ (SELECT list) of σ (WHERE predicate) of the FROM relation: ∏_{A1,A2}(σ_P(r)). SQL's SELECT = project; WHERE = select.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch3)** Which is true about duplicate handling in SQL vs relational algebra?
options: Relational algebra removes duplicates (set); SQL keeps them by default (multiset) unless DISTINCT is used
items.explain: TB2 Ch3: relational algebra uses set semantics (no duplicates); SQL uses multiset semantics and retains duplicates unless you write SELECT DISTINCT.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch1)** Which is listed as a major disadvantage of file-processing systems that database systems overcome?
options: Data redundancy and inconsistency, difficulty accessing data, and integrity/atomicity/concurrency/security problems
items.explain: TB2 Ch1 lists exactly these drawbacks of file systems: data redundancy & inconsistency, difficulty in accessing data, data isolation, integrity problems, atomicity problems, concurrent-access anomalies, and security problems.

items.q: **(Ramakrishnan & Gehrke, Ch4)** Over Sailors(sid,sname,rating,age), the expression ∏sname,rating(σ rating > 8 (Sailors)) returns:
options: The names and ratings of sailors whose rating exceeds 8
items.explain: σ rating>8 keeps the rows (sailors rated above 8); ∏sname,rating keeps just those two columns. Compose select (rows) then project (columns).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ch6)** A relationship set where the same entity set participates in different 'roles' (e.g. course as `course_id` and `prereq_id`) is a:
items.explain: TB2 Ch6: when an entity set participates more than once in a relationship set, it is recursive and explicit role names label the participation (e.g. prereq: course in role course_id and prereq_id).
